posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP decision-makers engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem as the real blocker, not AI itself, to signal deep domain understanding without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban isn't really about ChatGPT — it's about auditability. If you can't trace a number back to its source data, step by step, it doesn't matter how accurate it is. Regulators don't want confidence intervals, they want a paper trail. Wonder how many analytics teams are quietly in the same spot but haven't hit the regulator question yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consulting firm hitting the trust wall with Power BI — validate the real problem (trust, not tooling), add a sharp observation about why dashboards fail adoption
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the dashboard — it was wasted on the wrong problem. People don't stop using tools because they're hard to use, they stop using them because they don't trust where the numbers came from. Excel feels safer because everyone can see the formula. The real question is: what would it take for your finance team to trust a number they didn't personally calculate?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a confession that nobody made a hard call about what actually matters. The jump to 85% usage tells you everything — people don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because opening it feels like homework with no answer key. The real question isn't which 5 metrics you picked, it's how long it took before someone was willing to kill the other 42.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a governance problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone's technically empowered but nobody's actually aligned — and that gap doesn't close by adding more licences or better dashboards. The real issue is usually that 'revenue' was never properly defined before anyone touched a tool. Who owned that definition before Power BI showed up?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust/verification layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and most analytics vendors aren't ready for it. A hallucinated number in a dashboard isn't just wrong — it's an unvetted input that bypassed every control you'd normally have. We obsess over who can access data but almost nothing about whether the AI's interpretation of it can be trusted. Who in your org is actually signing off on AI-generated outputs before they move upstream?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with post about BI tools failing non-data users — validate the £200k waste pain, add the real diagnosis, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is painfully familiar. The dirty secret is most BI tools are essentially a second job — you have to learn the tool before the tool helps you do your actual job. And in a 50-person company, nobody has time for that second job. The question I keep asking is: who decided 'self-service' meant 'you can do it yourself if you know SQL'?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' wall — validate the culture diagnosis, add the layer about trust being the real casualty
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one very uncomfortable CFO — that's not a data problem, that's a trust problem. And once the CFO stops believing the dashboard, it takes a long time to win that back, even after you've fixed the underlying issue. The culture point is right, but I'd add: the tools often make it worse by making it too easy to 'personalise' a view without realising you've just forked the truth. How long did it take to actually trace which team had it right?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director diagnosing a real adoption failure with Copilot — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all. 'Nobody knows what to ask' is actually the whole game — it's not a Copilot problem, it's that most people don't have a clear enough mental model of their own data to know what question would even be useful. Shadow AI on phones is the symptom, but the disease is that the tool assumes a level of fluency that most orgs just haven't built yet. Do you think more training would move that needle, or is the interface itself the blocker?
